Your teacher discusses the ethics of data in class, so these questions check the basics: what makes a report unfair even when its numbers are right, and what you owe the people you collect data from. Every report and number here is made up for the task.

## Fair reporting

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 3: a report can be accurate and still be unfair, because of what it leaves out or how it frames the numbers."
tasks:

  - check: {"type":"question","q":"A company reports: \"Our drink has no added sugar!\" Another company's report on its own drink says: \"Cuts sugar by 40%!\" Both figures are true. Which is the most important ethical question to ask about each?","options":["What does the claim leave out, and who benefits from it being believed?","Which company has the bigger factory?","Whether the percentage is a whole number","How many people wrote the report"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"The size of the company isn't what makes a claim fair.","A whole-number percentage doesn't make a claim fair or unfair.","Who wrote it matters less than what it leaves out."],"explain":"A claim can be true and still misleading. ## Collecting data about people
```

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 3: collecting data from people carries duties of consent, privacy and avoiding harm."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"You want to find out how many hours your classmates sleep. Which plan is the most ethical?","options":["Ask volunteers to answer without their names, and tell them how the results will be used","Ask the whole class to say their hours out loud, one by one","Look at who is tired in class and record your guess","Ask teachers to read out each student's answers"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"People may feel pressure to answer, and everyone hears each answer.","A guess is not data, and recording it about named people is unfair to them.","The answers become public with names attached."],"explain":"Taking part should be voluntary, answers should not be traced to a person, and people should know what the data is for. ```teacher
```
```teacher
summary: A self-test on the fairness of reports and the care owed to people
  whose data is collected (AC9M10ST01, node 3, taught in class).
time: 10
timing: Fair reporting 5 min · Collecting data about people 5 min
goals:
  - I can say when a report is accurate but still unfair.
  - I can name how framing and leaving things out shape a claim.
  - I can say what people should be told and free to do before they give data.
before: >
  A Quick check: a few questions on what students should know for AC9M10ST01
  node 3, which you teach as a class discussion. It has no board, no clip and no
  new teaching, and it is optional, so it never holds up course completion.


  Use it as a self-test after your discussion, a starter, or revision. The
  discussion itself is the lesson. Node 3 asks students to name an ethical
  consideration beyond technical accuracy and to explain how an ethical or
  political framing has shaped a claim, so good class talk uses a real report
  that you have read yourself. This page uses made-up reports only; every number
  and organisation is invented.
running:
  - Before the questions, show two headlines that report the same number in
    different words and ask which one a reader would believe more.
  - After the second step, ask students what they would change about a survey
    they have already taken.
struggle: "Telling a true-but-misleading claim from a false one. Ask: is the
  number wrong, or is something left out or framed to push you?"
stuck:
  - see: A student says a report that uses correct numbers cannot be unethical.
    ask: Could a true number still leave out something that changes how you feel
      about it?
    fix: Yes. A correct number can be framed, selected or left without context so
      that it pushes a reader.
  - see: A student says anonymous data is always safe to share.
    ask: Could a question be harmful even if no names are attached?
    fix: Yes. Sensitive questions can cause harm or pressure, and in a small group
      an answer may point to one person.
stretch: Find a news headline that reports a statistic. Say what it frames, what
  it leaves out and who gains if you believe it.
support: Give two sentences that report the same number with different words and
  ask which words push the reader.
leads: >
  Back in class: a discussion of a real report you have read; the sleep
  investigation brief on the Data and chance briefs page raises consent and
  privacy when collecting data from classmates.
exit:
  q: Name one way a report can be accurate and still unfair.
  a: It leaves out some results, frames the numbers to push a reader, uses a
    misleading scale, overstates what a small sample shows, or hides who paid
    for it.
explain: >
  A report can have correct numbers and still be unfair: what it leaves out, how
  it frames the numbers, and who gains from it all shape the claim.


  When you collect data from people, taking part should be voluntary, they
  should know how it will be used, and the results should not point to any one
  person.
```
